title: TypeScript SDK: Duplex Stream Bridge playbook (AsyncIterable <-> Web Streams, backpressure, retries)
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem statement: Customers increasingly use Redwood's TypeScript SDK in two styles: AsyncIterable consumers (typical Node SDK idioms) and Web Streams consumers (browser fetch/Streams API and some platform runtimes). Inconsistent semantics between the two shapes (cancellation timing, backpressure semantics, retry idempotency hooks) produce surprising behaviors and subtle resource leaks in production.

Goal: Produce a developer-facing playbook and API proposal for a Duplex Stream Bridge that provides robust, well-documented interoperability between AsyncIterable and Web Streams for streaming generation in the TypeScript SDK. The playbook should: (1) define cancellation/cutover semantics, (2) define explicit backpressure contracts and buffering defaults, (3) propose retry hooks and idempotency metadata for resumable streams, (4) include ergonomic helper factories for common patterns, and (5) include end-to-end examples and tests.

Scope: TypeScript SDK runtime surface (not core Go runtime). Deliverables: API proposals (2 variants), backwards-compatible shim implementation, migration guide, example snippets (Node + browser), unit & integration tests, perf microbench plan, and documentation/FAQ.

Acceptance criteria: 
- API variant chosen by consensus and documented in the PR.
- Shim converts AsyncIterable consumers to Web ReadableStream and vice-versa with deterministic cancellation propagation.
- Streaming examples for Node (AsyncIterator consumer) and Browser (ReadableStream pipeTo) included in docs.
- Retry hook support that can attach idempotency tokens per-request and allows resume from last acked token when the server exposes token-based checkpoints.
- End-to-end test demonstrating cancellation, backpressure (slow consumer), and single-request retry without duplication.
- Benchmark results showing <10% median token-latency overhead vs native AsyncIterable for small batches (1-4 tokens) and acceptable memory behavior under load.

Proposed ergonomics (short):
- export function bridgeAsyncIterableToReadable<T>(src: AsyncIterable<T>, options?): ReadableStream<T>
- export function bridgeReadableToAsyncIterable<T>(rs: ReadableStream<T>, options?): AsyncIterable<T>
- options: { highWaterMark?: number, bufferStrategy?: "sliding" | "fixed", onResumeToken?: (token:string)=>void, onCheckpointAck?: (token:string)=>void }

Trade-offs considered:
- Fully automatic resume vs explicit idempotency tokens: chose opt-in resume with explicit token callbacks to avoid silent duplication when models or endpoints behave non-idempotently.
- Memory vs latency: default to modest HWM=2 for low-latency interactive flows; allow configurable buffer for batchy use-cases.

Implementation notes:
- Avoid exposing internal runtime queues; implement the shim using platform primitives (ReadableStream controller + async iteration loop).
- Use AbortSignal for cancellation propagation. Ensure both ends observe the same AbortSignal where possible.
- Document the difference between consumer-cancel (user closed stream) and producer-finished (EOF) semantics.

Migration guide highlights:
- For existing consumers that use for-await (AsyncIterable), no change needed if bridge functions are not used.
- For browser clients using fetch + ReadableStream, recommend bridgeReadableToAsyncIterable when reusing server-side streams logic.
